name: Perl
year_note: Perl 1.0 was released on 18 December 1987. Perl 5 (October 1994), a near-rewrite that added references, objects, modules and lexical variables, is the language still in use; 'Perl 6' became the separate language Raku.
tagline: The Unix text-processing workhorse and glue of the early Web: regexes built into the syntax, and more than one way to do it.
summary: Perl is a dynamically typed, interpreted scripting language that fused C, sed, awk and the Unix shell into one general-purpose tool for text processing and system administration. Regular expressions, hashes and string interpolation are part of its syntax, and sigils ($, @, %) plus scalar/list context let dense one-liners do a great deal. It was the leading language for CGI web programming in the mid-1990s, and its regular-expression dialect became a de facto standard that many later languages copied.
history:
Larry Wall began Perl in 1987 while working as a programmer at Unisys, as a Unix scripting language to make report processing easier than juggling awk, sed and shell scripts; version 1.0 was released on 18 December 1987. Perl 2 (1988) brought an improved regex engine, Perl 3 (1989) handled binary data, and Perl 4 (1991) was released to coincide with the first edition of 'Programming Perl', the 'Camel Book'.

Perl 5 (October 1994) added references, lexical `my` variables, closures, packages as modules and a minimalist object system built on `bless`, and CPAN went online in 1995 as its central module archive. Perl became the standard language for CGI scripts in the mid-1990s and was called the 'duct tape that holds the Internet together'.

In 2000 Wall announced Perl 6 as a ground-up redesign; it grew into a separate language and was renamed Raku in 2019. Perl 5 kept evolving through yearly releases: 5.10 (2007) added `say`, named captures and the defined-or operator `//`, 5.36 (2022) made subroutine signatures stable, 5.38 (2023) introduced an experimental native `class` syntax, and 5.40 (2024) stabilised `try`/`catch`.
innovations: Regular expressions as first-class syntax (=~, m//, s///, tr///) with interpolation, captures into variables and the implicit $_ topic
The Perl 5 regex extensions (non-greedy quantifiers, lookaround, /x commented patterns) that PCRE (1997) packaged and Python, Java, JavaScript and PHP adopted
CPAN (online since 1995): a mirrored, language-wide archive of reusable modules, the counterpart that PyPI, RubyGems and npm later provided for their languages
Sigils and context: the same expression yields different results in scalar and list context
Taint mode (-T), which marks data from outside the program as untrusted until it is explicitly checked
Established the dynamic 'glue language' for Unix system administration and CGI web programming

typing.notes: Scalars convert freely between strings and numbers depending on the operator (`.` vs `+`, `eq` vs `==`); sigils mark container kind (scalar, array, hash) rather than type.

influenced_by.note: Expression syntax, operators, braces and printf-style formatting; Perl aimed to replace mixtures of C, sh and awk.

Perl 1.0 was pitched at problems that 'would ordinarily use sed or awk or sh': associative arrays, the -n input loop and <> 'somewhat like sed -n or awk', the .. line-range operator, and the a2p awk-to-Perl translator it shipped with.

influenced_by_external.name: sed
influenced_by_external.note: s/// substitution and the regex-driven line-editing model.

influenced_by_external.name: Unix shell (sh)
influenced_by_external.note: $-prefixed variables, string interpolation, here-documents and backticks.

structured-control.note: Also statement modifiers (`print if $x`, `... for @list`) and `unless`/`until`.

block-scope.note: Lexical `my` variables; earlier versions had only dynamically scoped `local`.

exceptions.note: `die` with `eval {}` blocks (any value, including objects, can be thrown); a native `try`/`catch` arrived experimentally in 5.34 and became stable in 5.40 (2024).

tail-calls.note: No automatic tail-call elimination, but `goto &sub` explicitly replaces the current call frame.

classes.note: Classes are packages and objects are references `bless`ed into them; Moose/Moo are the common frameworks, and 5.38 added an experimental native `class`/`field`/`method` syntax.

inheritance.note: Multiple inheritance through the package's @ISA array (`use parent`); C3 method resolution optional since 5.10.

traits-mixins.note: Roles via Moose, Moo or Role::Tiny on CPAN.

abstract-data-types.note: Blessed hashes expose their internals; hiding needs closures, inside-out objects or the private `field`s of the newer class syntax.

modules.note: Packages in .pm files loaded with `use`, with Exporter-controlled imports; CPAN distributes them.

first-class-functions.note: Code references and anonymous `sub { ... }`; map, grep and sort take blocks.

reference-counting.note: Deterministic destruction; there is no cycle collector, so circular structures leak unless broken with Scalar::Util::weaken.

reflection.note: Symbol tables (stashes) and typeglobs can be inspected and modified at run time; `ref`, `can`, `isa` and string `eval`.

compile-time-execution.note: BEGIN blocks and `use` run ordinary Perl code during compilation, e.g. to generate subroutines or constants.

regex-builtin.note: Match, substitute and transliterate operators with interpolated patterns; Perl's dialect became the model for PCRE.

milestones.event: Perl 1.0 released by Larry Wall (18 December)
Perl 4 and the first edition of 'Programming Perl' (the Camel Book)
Perl 5: references, objects, modules, lexical variables and closures
Perl 6 announced as a ground-up redesign
Perl 5.10: say, named captures, defined-or //, given/when
Perl 6 renamed Raku, leaving 'Perl' to Perl 5

trivia: Wall first called the language 'Pearl', then dropped the 'a' after learning of an existing language named PEARL; 'Practical Extraction and Report Language' is a backronym.
Its motto 'There's more than one way to do it' is abbreviated TMTOWTDI and pronounced 'Tim Toady'.
The first edition of 'Programming Perl' (1991) had a camel on the cover, so it is known as the Camel Book.

hello.notes: Since 5.10, `use feature 'say'` (or `use v5.10`) enables `say`, which appends the newline itself.

factorial.notes: Signatures became stable in 5.36; older code unpacks the argument list by hand with `my ($n) = @_;`.

fizzbuzz.notes: `$i % 3` is false (0) for multiples of 3, and `$word || $i` falls back to the number when the string is empty.

higher-order.notes: grep and map take a block and a list and alias $_ to each element; an array interpolated in a string is joined with $" (a space by default).

shapes.notes: `ref` returns the class a reference was blessed into, and `->area` looks the method up in that package. Perl 5.38's experimental `class` feature offers declarative `field`s and `method`s instead of bless.

signature.notes: `while (<DATA>)` reads the lines after __DATA__ into $_, and a bare /.../ matches against $_. Captures land in $1..$3, /x allows whitespace inside the pattern, and s{...}{...}g rewrites every match in place.

toolchains.notes: Preinstalled on most Linux distributions and macOS; all snippets also ran on 5.38.

browser.notes: perl 5 compiled to WebAssembly with Emscripten; self-described beta and not actively updated.

runtime.notes: The official Docker image is the dependable sandbox; the in-browser option is experimental.
